newsitem.title: CHINA: China warns officials on sale of government posts.
newsitem.headline: China warns officials on sale of government posts.

text.p: China on Tuesday fired another salvo in its battle against graft, targeting political corruption by warning government officials not to take bribes for appointing people to jobs.

The Central Commission for Discipline Inspection of the ruling Communist Party had recently issued a notice blasting the sale of government posts as a serious offence that sullied the party's image, the Xinhua news agency said.
Analysts said the notice was the latest push by Beijing to crack down on rampant corruption among government officials.
"This sort of warning is aimed at political corruption rather than economic corruption and so is much more serious," said a Chinese analyst who declined to be identified.

Chinese President Jiang Zemin has called graft a virus that threatens the party's grip on power, and Beijing has repeatedly launched anti-corruption battles aimed at exposing officials who barter their bureaucratic clout for economic gain.
Officials in China can wield enormous power, and many people eager for the influence and prestige of a post have tried to bribe their way into government positions.
The notice called on officials to learn from the fate of two officials who were punished for accepting bribes in exchange for promoting or appointing others to government positions, Xinhua said.

One county official in central Jiangxi province was sentenced to 13 years in jail and stripped of his party membership for taking bribes totalling more than 130,000 yuan ($15,600), while another in Shanxi province was kicked out of the party and disciplined, the agency said.

"Officials and party groups at every level should learn a deep lesson...and adopt strong measures to resolutely punish the corrupt actions of buying and selling official positions," it quoted the notice as saying.

The warning followed a move by Beijing on Monday to tighten control over officials by requiring them to report the financial affairs of their families as well as marriages or business involving foreigners.
Chinese officials have found new opportunities to boost their power as economic reforms loosen Beijing's authoritarian rule.
Last September, China ordered all central government officials to report their incomes as well as any benefits, gifts or other sources of income.
